title: Kartarpur Sahib

lines: A WHITE GURDWARA IN THE FIELDS.
cards: A pair of hands, cracked at the knuckles, soil under the nails. A tea glass on a wall at the edge of a field. Somewhere a tractor coughs and goes quiet.
In flat farmland near the river Ravi, a white gurdwara rises out of the green, and the fields come almost up to its walls. Yesterday, where Guru Nanak's life began.
Today, where it ended, and what he did with the years between: he went home to the soil.

teach.b: First, the place. Kartarpur, the Creator's town, as year one told.
Tradition says Guru Nanak settled here after his long journeys, farmed his own land, gathered a community around hymns, work and a shared kitchen, and died here.
Today the gurdwara stands among fields on the Pakistani side of the border, and pilgrims come through the corridor this path met on an earlier day. Second, the hymn.

teach.h: MIND THE FARMER, BODY THE FIELD.
teach.b: In Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak turns a farmer's work into a picture of the inner life, in paraphrase: make your mind the farmer, good deeds the work, effort the water, and your body the field. Sow the Name as the seed.
Let contentment be the plank that levels the soil, and humility the fence around it. It's practical: a farmer can't skip the water or forget the fence, and neither, in the hymn, can a seeker.
Third, why it matters that he farmed. After all those roads, the great teacher could have lived on gifts.

Tradition says he chose a plow. So when Sikhs speak of earning by honest work, they can point to a field and say, that's where he farmed. Fourth, the end of the story, told briefly because year one told it fully.
Tradition says that when he died here, Hindus and Muslims who both loved him laid flowers on either side of him.

teach.h: A MEMORIAL AND A GRAVE, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Today a memorial and a grave stand side by side at Kartarpur.
A field, a hymn about a field, and a farmer people of two faiths wouldn't let go.

how: Pilgrims visit Gurdwara Kartarpur Sahib, across the border in Pakistan, through the Kartarpur corridor; Sikhs remember it as the place where Guru Nanak farmed, built a community and died.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, home after long journeys. people would gladly support you with gifts. how do you live?
o: accept the gifts and keep teaching.
settle at Kartarpur and farm your own land.
games.why: tradition says he settled at Kartarpur and farmed, with hymns at dawn and dusk and a shared kitchen.

practice: See flat green land running to the edge of sight, a white gurdwara in the middle, and a man in plain clothes walking a furrow early, before the heat.

Then walk your own field for a minute, the mind as the farmer and the body as the field, and just notice what seed you're sowing today and what fence keeps it safe. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.
